answer:
Auto Layout is a constraint-based layout engine. You declare relationships between views (e.g. "top of A is 16pt below bottom of B") and the system solves them every layout pass to compute concrete frames.

### Vs frame-based
- Adapts to size classes, dynamic type, rotation, multitasking, RTL.
- Same code works across devices — no per-screen frame math.
- Slower than raw frames at extreme scale (10k+ views), but plenty fast for normal apps.

### Three constraint APIs from Apple
- NSLayoutConstraint(item:...) — verbose, original.
- **NSLayoutAnchor** — fluent, type-safe (modern recommended).
- **UIStackView** — composes flow layouts without explicit constraints.

Third-party DSLs (SnapKit, PinLayout) add more sugar but anchors usually suffice.

A view's intrinsic content size is the size it wants to be based on its own content — a label sized to its text, a button to its title plus insets.

Auto Layout treats it as a pair of default width and height constraints, and two priorities decide who yields when the row is too narrow:

- **Content hugging** — resistance to growing larger than the intrinsic size. Higher means the view stays small.
- **Compression resistance** — resistance to shrinking below the intrinsic size. Higher means the view stays large.

Defaults are 250 for hugging and 750 for compression resistance, identical on every view, which is why two labels sharing a row produce an ambiguous layout until you break the tie. Give the title a lower compression resistance than the badge and the title truncates while the badge keeps its full width.

A custom view joins in by overriding `intrinsicContentSize`, and it must call `invalidateIntrinsicContentSize()` whenever its content changes — otherwise Auto Layout keeps solving against the stale measurement.

UIStackView generates the constraints between its arranged subviews for you: you set an axis, a distribution and an alignment, then constrain only the stack itself.

### Key properties
- **axis** — .horizontal / .vertical
- **distribution** — .fill, .fillEqually, .fillProportionally, .equalSpacing, .equalCentering
- **alignment** — .leading, .center, .trailing, .fill (the perpendicular axis)
- **spacing** — a fixed gap, or `setCustomSpacing(_:after:)` for one child

The property that earns its keep is `isHidden` on a child: the stack removes the slot and closes the gap, with no constraint of your own to activate or deactivate. Doing that by hand means toggling constraints and is where most "unable to satisfy" logs come from.

Nesting stacks models most screens cleanly — it is the same idea as flexbox in CSS or Column/Row in Compose. The cost is a deeper view hierarchy, so for very large scrolling grids a compositional collection view layout beats stacks inside cells.

Safe area is the region of the screen NOT covered by system UI: status bar, navigation bar, tab bar, home indicator, and notches/cutouts on modern iPhones. Anchoring content to the safe area keeps it visible regardless of device.

- `view.safeAreaLayoutGuide` — UILayoutGuide whose anchors describe the safe area for that view.
- `view.safeAreaInsets` — the inset values (top/leading/bottom/trailing).
- Override `safeAreaInsetsDidChange()` to react.
- Use `additionalSafeAreaInsets` on a UIViewController to push your content past a custom overlay (e.g. a floating banner).

When Auto Layout can't find a valid solution it prints a long diagnostic and breaks one constraint. To investigate:

- **Read the diagnostic** — it lists every involved constraint, with addresses; pause the running app and `po` each constraint to find the offender.
- **Identifier** — set `constraint.identifier = "contentBottom"` so the log names them.
- Symbolic breakpoint on `UIViewAlertForUnsatisfiableConstraints` — the debugger pauses at the very moment the conflict is detected.
- View Debugger (Xcode → Debug → View Debugging → Capture View Hierarchy) — visualize the tree, inspect constraints, see ambiguous frames in red.
- `view.hasAmbiguousLayout` and `view.exerciseAmbiguityInLayout()` — toggle ambiguous views to spot which one floats.
- Set lower priority (e.g. 999) on optional constraints to mark which one is allowed to break.

`setNeedsLayout` schedules a layout pass, `layoutIfNeeded` runs one immediately, and `layoutSubviews` is the callback UIKit invokes during that pass — you call the first two and override the third.

- `setNeedsLayout()` — marks the view dirty and returns straight away; UIKit lays it out before the next frame is drawn. Cheap, and safe to call repeatedly.
- `layoutIfNeeded()` — forces the pending layout to happen now, synchronously, for the view and its subtree. Use it only when you need the new frames in this turn of the run loop.
- `layoutSubviews()` — never call it directly. Override it for what Auto Layout cannot express: a CAGradientLayer's frame, a mask path, a corner radius derived from the final height.

The standard animation recipe: change the constraint constants, then call `layoutIfNeeded()` inside a `UIView.animate` block so UIKit interpolates between the old and new layouts instead of snapping to the new one.

The matching pair for drawing is `setNeedsDisplay()` and `draw(_:)`; layout and drawing are separate passes, and calling the layout methods will not redraw anything.

A view created in code still has `translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints` set to `true`, which turns its frame and autoresizing mask into real constraints that fight the ones you wrote.

- With the flag on, UIKit generates an `NSAutoresizingMaskLayoutConstraint` set pinning the view to its current frame. A programmatic view starts at `.zero`, so those constraints say "be zero-sized at the origin" — which is why everything ends up in the corner.
- Your constraints and the synthesised ones cannot both hold, so the engine breaks some of them and logs the familiar "Unable to simultaneously satisfy constraints" wall. Seeing `NSAutoresizingMaskLayoutConstraint` in that log is the tell.
- Set the flag to `false` on every view you position with constraints, and only on those views.

Where you must leave it alone: a view controller's root view, a table or collection cell's `contentView`, and any view you deliberately lay out by frame. UIKit owns those. Interface Builder already sets it to `false` for views in a nib, and `UIStackView` sets it for its arranged subviews, which is one more reason stacks are less error-prone.

The habit that removes the whole class of bug is a small factory or an `addSubview` helper that turns the flag off as the view is created, so no call site has to remember.

The autoresizing mask itself — the old springs-and-struts system with `.flexibleWidth` and `.flexibleHeight` — still works, and is perfectly reasonable for a small frame-based view. It just cannot be mixed with Auto Layout on the same view.

A self-sizing cell needs an unbroken chain of vertical constraints from the top of `contentView` to its bottom, so Auto Layout can solve for the height instead of falling back on a fixed one.

- Every subview must be linked into that chain: top pinned, each gap defined, and the last view pinned to the bottom. One missing bottom constraint and the height is ambiguous, so the cell collapses to the estimated value.
- Constraints belong on `contentView`, not on the cell itself.
- A multi-line label needs `numberOfLines = 0` and both horizontal edges pinned, because its height cannot be computed until its width is known.
- Nothing in the chain may contradict the content — a fixed height constraint on a label defeats the whole mechanism.
- `rowHeight = UITableView.automaticDimension` with a non-zero `estimatedRowHeight` has been the default for years, so the flags are rarely the bug.

The classic warning is a conflict at the moment a cell is created, before it has been given its real height. Giving the bottom constraint priority 999 lets it yield for that one pass instead of breaking something you care about, and the log stays quiet.

Collection views work the same way, with the estimate expressed in the layout: `.estimated(88)` in a compositional layout, or `UICollectionViewCompositionalLayout.list(using:)` when you want table-like rows.

Two payoffs come free once the chain is right: the cell resizes itself when the user raises the text size, and you can assert on the height in a unit test with `systemLayoutSizeFitting` rather than scrolling and eyeballing it.

A scroll view computes its content size from its subviews' constraints, so the content has to be pinned to `contentLayoutGuide` on all four edges and take its width from `frameLayoutGuide`.

- `contentLayoutGuide` describes the scrollable area — constraints to it determine `contentSize`.
- `frameLayoutGuide` describes the scroll view's visible frame — constraints to it determine what stays fixed on screen.
- **The recipe**: pin a single container view or stack view to all four edges of the content guide, then add `container.widthAnchor == scrollView.frameLayoutGuide.widthAnchor` for vertical scrolling, or the height equivalent for horizontal.

That width constraint is the step people skip, and it is the reason a scroll view either shows nothing or scrolls sideways for no visible reason: without it the container's width is unconstrained, so the layout is ambiguous in both axes.

Inside the container everything still needs a full top-to-bottom chain, exactly as in a self-sizing cell — a vertical `UIStackView` gives you that for free and is the fastest correct version.

### Two details that come up in practice
- `contentInset` is what you set, `adjustedContentInset` is what the system actually applies after safe area and bars. Read the adjusted value when computing offsets, and set `contentInsetAdjustmentBehavior = .never` when you want raw control.
- For the keyboard, constrain to `view.keyboardLayoutGuide` instead of parsing keyboard notification frames yourself; it animates in step with the keyboard and handles the hardware-keyboard cases.
code_example:
let scrollView = UIScrollView()
let content = UIStackView()          // one container, pinned to the content guide
content.axis = .vertical
content.spacing = 16
[scrollView, content].forEach { $0.translatesAutoresizingMaskIntoConstraints = false }
view.addSubview(scrollView)
scrollView.addSubview(content)

NSLayoutConstraint.activate([
  scrollView.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.safeAreaLayoutGuide.topAnchor),
  scrollView.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.leadingAnchor),
  scrollView.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.trailingAnchor),
  scrollView.bottomAnchor.constraint(equalTo: view.bottomAnchor),

  // contentLayoutGuide drives contentSize: all four edges, no exceptions
  content.topAnchor.constraint(equalTo: scrollView.contentLayoutGuide.topAnchor),
  content.leadingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: scrollView.contentLayoutGuide.leadingAnchor),
  content.trailingAnchor.constraint(equalTo: scrollView.contentLayoutGuide.trailingAnchor),
  content.bottomAnchor.constraint(equalTo: scrollView.contentLayoutGuide.bottomAnchor),

  // frameLayoutGuide fixes the width, leaving only the height free to grow
  content.widthAnchor.constraint(equalTo: scrollView.frameLayoutGuide.widthAnchor),
])

// Keyboard: constrain to the keyboard guide instead of parsing notification frames
view.keyboardLayoutGuide.topAnchor
  .constraint(greaterThanOrEqualTo: content.bottomAnchor, constant: 16).isActive = true

// When computing offsets, read adjustedContentInset — it already includes bars and safe area
let visibleTop = scrollView.contentOffset.y + scrollView.adjustedContentInset.top

answer:
Change the `constant` for anything you would animate, swap active constraints for a structural change, and change priority only to decide which of two competing constraints wins.

- `constant` — keep a reference to the constraint, assign the new value, then run `layoutIfNeeded()` inside an animation block. This is the cheapest option and the only one that animates cleanly.
- **Activation** — build both sets once, then `NSLayoutConstraint.deactivate(old)` and `activate(new)`. Use it when the relationships themselves differ, not just the numbers.
- **Priority** — for a constraint that should hold when it can and yield when it cannot: a preferred width alongside a required trailing edge, or a 999-priority constraint that survives a temporary conflict.

The bug worth naming is creating new constraints on every update instead of reusing them. Nothing complains at first; the old ones stay installed, the layout gets slower each time, and eventually two of them contradict each other and the log fills with broken constraints. If you find yourself calling `constraint(equalTo:)` inside an update method, that is the smell.

A few specifics: you cannot change a priority to or from `.required` on an already-installed constraint — it traps. Batch several changes and call `layoutIfNeeded()` once. And for the common case of showing and hiding something, setting `isHidden` on a `UIStackView`'s arranged subview beats all three, because the stack removes the slot and closes the gap with no constraint work at all.

Pinning to the edge gives you the literal bounds, `layoutMarginsGuide` adds the view's own margins, and `readableContentGuide` caps the width so a paragraph does not run edge to edge on a large screen.

- Margins are set with `directionalLayoutMargins`, which uses leading and trailing so it mirrors in right-to-left languages. A view controller's root view also gets a system minimum that follows the device, and `viewRespectsSystemMinimumLayoutMargins = false` is how you go narrower.
- `readableContentGuide` is much narrower than the view on iPad, which is exactly the point: body text stays readable while a full-bleed image still pins to the edges.
- `safeAreaLayoutGuide` is a different concern — it keeps content out from under the bars and the home indicator, and you often combine it with margins rather than choosing between them.
- A `UIStackView` ignores its own margins until you set `isLayoutMarginsRelativeArrangement = true`.

The other guide worth knowing is `UILayoutGuide` itself: an invisible rectangle you can constrain to. Use one wherever you would otherwise add a transparent spacer view to create a gap or align a group. It costs nothing to draw, receives no touches, adds no accessibility element, and keeps the view hierarchy honest about what is actually on screen.

Use leading and trailing anchors instead of left and right, and let text drive height instead of hard-coding it — those two habits prevent most of the damage.

### Right-to-left
- `leadingAnchor` and `trailingAnchor` mirror automatically; `leftAnchor` and `rightAnchor` never do. The same split exists between `NSDirectionalEdgeInsets` and `UIEdgeInsets`.
- Directional glyphs such as a back chevron need `imageFlippedForRightToLeftLayoutDirection()`, or the mirroring option in the asset catalog.
- Some controls must not mirror at all — media transport, a numeric keypad, a chart axis. Set `semanticContentAttribute` to `.playback`, `.spatial` or `.forceLeftToRight` on those.
- Test with the scheme's right-to-left pseudolanguage rather than trusting a review.

### Dynamic Type
- `font = .preferredFont(forTextStyle:)` plus `adjustsFontForContentSizeCategory = true`. For a brand font, wrap it in `UIFontMetrics` so it scales the same way, and scale hard-coded spacing with `scaledValue(for:)`.
- `numberOfLines = 0` and no fixed heights, so intrinsic content size does the work.
- At accessibility sizes, switch a horizontal stack to vertical. React to the change by registering for the content-size-category trait rather than overriding `traitCollectionDidChange`, which is deprecated.

The same discipline covers localisation generally: German strings run roughly a third longer than English, so a button sized to a hardcoded width is a bug waiting for a translator to find it.
